prospect.name: Jacob Reyf
prospect.location: Not cleanly established. He said 'Mexico City time zone, which is central time' and the rep restated it as Mountain time without resolving the contradiction. His phone number carries a +1 305 (Miami) area code.
prospect.occupation: Owner or principal of an auto finance company he started in 2013 — 'we finance cars. We're a bank, basically.' Fewer than 20 employees, currently adding technology to processes to drive growth, which is why he describes it as a startup. On the computer all the time, working Monday through Sunday.
prospect.family_status: Married. Wife cooks healthy at home, is described as very slim at about 100 pounds, fit and training herself. In-laws travelling to Italy this summer.
prospect.training_background: Has trained daily since age 15, roughly twenty years of starting the day with a workout. Ran the conventional split for years — back and biceps, chest and triceps, push-pull. Has done many online programmes. Has used kettlebells before but only folded into other sessions — swings, some snatches — never a full kettlebell programme. For the last two weeks has been training by copying Trevor's kettlebell videos off Instagram with no plan behind it. Plays backgammon semi-professionally and travels for tournaments.
prospect.medical: Broke his wrist at some point; states it has not affected him and is not a limitation. Reports the kettlebell hitting his forearm on snatches is 'a little uncomfortable'. Explicitly confirmed no injuries affecting day-to-day life and no chronic conditions in the family.

signals: Business owner running an auto finance company, self-funded and unhesitating — paid $6,000 in full on the call within minutes of hearing the number
Already fit and training daily for twenty years; nothing about this is a rescue
Price was a quality signal, not a barrier — his only pricing question was about convenience of structure, and when offered a 50/50 split he took the rep's advice and paid the lot
Explicitly values specialisation over cost: 'You can hire a trainer anywhere. They all do the same. That's the problem.'
Arrived pre-sold — 'I'm here because I'm sold, by the way' — and told the rep to skip the persuasion and give him the price

goals.text: Build a long-term, sustainable kettlebell routine he can hold for a lifetime rather than another programme he abandons
Train efficiently — in and out in 20 to 30 minutes, because he does not enjoy spending time in the gym and resents leaving work to go
Combine mobility with weightlifting in one session, which he believes kettlebells uniquely deliver
Train anywhere with one piece of equipment — outside, in a gym, in a small Italian town with no gym
Live a healthy lifestyle for its own sake and for longevity, with no competitive or aesthetic target
Work out because it feels good mentally and because it is how he wants to start the day
Have a structured plan instead of clicking random videos on Trevor's Instagram
Learn the kettlebell foundations properly, specifically to fix the snatch

pains.text: Has stopped enjoying training — 'thinking about leaving what I'm doing to go work out, it just... I'm just like I don't want to do it'
No plan — 'otherwise I'm just going to his Instagram, I'm clicking on a random video'
Does not want to have to think about programming himself — 'My problem is, I don't want to think'
Cannot find a specialist — 'You can hire a trainer anywhere. They all do the same. That's the problem. And there's no one really focused and specialized in something'
Works on a computer Monday through Sunday and finds the gym has become an extra chore competing with work he actually enjoys
Travels once or twice a month and intercontinentally every three months, with no solution for training on the road — 'I'm going to be in a small town, there's definitely no gym... What do I do?'
Burned by a previous online programme's nutrition promise — 'I tried this program online, and they sold me on, you can still eat whatever you want'
Calorie counting proved unsustainable when he tried it
Ageing out of the conventional split — 'you get older, you want mobility'
Kettlebell hits the forearm uncomfortably on snatches

objections.raw_quote: I'm sure you deal with a lot of people and this whole, like, watch the videos before you come to the call, so you're prepared to pay. Like, I get that. I've done, I've been through many calls like this, and I don't do the hard sell. I do, like, I kind of do it on my terms.
objections.rep_response: Did not argue. Agreed with the frame and handed control back — 'at the end of the day, it's not, it's your decision, not mine' — then added a genuine disqualification hypothesis: 'I don't want to sell you something that's not aligned with you at all... maybe there is a hypothesis that this isn't for you, to be honest.' The prospect immediately relaxed.

objections.raw_quote: okay okay okay okay I like it but I can't pay monthly you can but what like you want to pay monthly I would I would prefer to pay monthly
objections.rep_response: Offered a four-option menu — upfront as the cheapest, a 50/50 split of $3,000 today and $3,000 in 30 days, six monthly payments of $1,200, or third-party financing through a provider he named as Pava with interest and up to twelve months. Then talked the prospect off the split and onto full payment: 'No, but half, in 30 days, it means nothing. It's the same thing.' Proposed label: payment_structure_preference.

offer.payment_plan_terms: Four structures offered live: (1) pay in full up front, described as the cheapest; (2) 50/50 — $3,000 on the call and $3,000 in 30 days; (3) six monthly payments of $1,200, a total of $7,200, with the total never stated; (4) third-party financing through a provider named as 'Pava', interest-bearing, term dependent on credit score, up to twelve months. Prospect took option 1.

evidence: Payment was made and verified live on the call — the rep dropped the link into the Zoom chat, the prospect confirmed receipt, and the rep then said 'okay paid oh okay let me just double check yep'.
Paid in full for the six-month programme at $6,000: 'So we're on it up front, the whole thing.' / 'Yeah.' Prospect confirmed the link scope — 'So this is for six months, yeah?' / 'Yep, correct.'
Onboarding call with Trevor booked for 11:15am the following day, after payment cleared.
Prospect confirmed receipt of both the onboarding confirmation email and the agreement email, plus a welcome email.

Counter-evidence on process quality, not on the outcome: the prospect closed himself. He asked for the price twice before the rep offered it — 'all the build-up, you build up and you get me so excited. What's the price?' — and had declared himself sold in the second minute.
Counter-evidence: the agreement was not signed on the call. The rep accepted 'you can do it later today' and affirmed the prospect's statement that he would not read it.
outcome.next_step: Onboarding call with Trevor at 11:15am the following day. Prospect to sign the agreement and complete the onboarding form before that call; Trevor takes roughly 24 hours after onboarding to map the programme.

notable.note: The clearest example in the batch of a call that closed cleanly and ran badly. The prospect arrived pre-sold, named his own pain, named his own gap and asked for the price — the rep ran no consequence frame, no commitment check, no root-cause work, and explicitly closed off the deep-why line by summarising the goal as 'just for health and longevity was not, nothing, nothing more'. The qualifying question about the prospect's business was asked after the money had been taken. Two things to compare across the corpus: the six-month instalment option totals $7,200 and that total was never spoken, and the guarantee that was volunteered to another prospect on the same day was not mentioned here at all.

quality.notes: Severe. Whole passages invert, and the entire price presentation from roughly 00:20:01 to 00:21:02 is collapsed into a single unbroken block attributed to the prospect while containing both sides of the exchange, including the rep's payment-option menu. The rep's frame-agreement check 'Is that perfect?' is labelled to the prospect; the prospect's question 'are you training me or he's training me?' is labelled to the rep. The transcript opens with 'Recording stopped', and there are unexplained silent gaps around the payment processing at 00:24-00:26 and again at 00:29-00:30. Roles read from content throughout.
